MISHNAH 6

If a woman says: I commit myself to a set of birds if I give birth to a male child, and she gave birth to a male child — she brings two sets of birds, one for her vow and another for her obligation. If she gave them to the kohen who must offer three birds above and one below, and he did not do so, but offered two above and two below, and he did not consult — she must bring another bird which is offered above; when of one kind. When of two kinds — she must bring two. If she specified her vow she must bring another three birds; when of one kind. When of two kinds — she brings four. If she designated her vow, she must bring another five birds; when of one kind. When of two kinds — she must bring six. If she gave them to the kohen and it is not known what she gave and the kohen offered them and the manner in which they were offered is not known — she must bring another four birds for her vow, and two for her obligation, and one sin-offering; Ben Azzai says, Two sin-offerings. Said Rabbi Yehoshua, This is what they have said: while it lives it has one voice, when it dies, seven voices; How are there seven voices? Its two horns, two trumpets; its two leg-bones, two flutes; its skin for a drum; its large intestines for lyres; its small intestines for harps. And some say, Also its wool for tekhelet. Rabbi Shimon ben Akashia says, Aging ignoramuses, the older they become, the more their minds agitate them as it is said: (Job 12:20) “He removes the speech of men of trust and takes away the sense of the elders.” But not so with the Torah elders, who the older they become, the more their minds become settled, as it is said: (ibid. 12) “With aged men there is wisdom and understanding in the length of days.”

Kehati

האשה שאמרה If a woman said: I commit myself to — offer — a set of birds if I give birth to a male child — in addition to the pair of birds a needy woman is required to bring — one pigeon for a sin-offering and one for a burnt-offering upon giving birth. The birds she vowed to offer upon the birth of her male child are offered as burnt-offerings since a sin-offering cannot be offered as a freewill-offering (see Introduction to our Tractate)

and she gave birth to a male child — and must fulfill her vow — she brings two sets of birds, one for her vow and another for her obligation — i.e., two burnt-offerings and the obligatory offering — a sin-offering and burnt-offering.

נתנם לכהן If she gave them — the four birds— to the kohen — as unspecified offerings — who must offer three birds — of these, two pairs above and one below the ḥut hasikra. The two sets she brought contain three burnt-offerings and one sin-offering.

לא עשה כן And he did not do so, but offered two above and two below — the kohen treated both as obligatory offerings. And he did not consult the woman regarding the status of the two pairs of birds and thus erred in his performance,

צריכה להביא she must bring another bird — her burnt-offering offered below being invalid — which is offered above — where burnt-offerings belong. When does the above apply? When all four birds are of one kind — i.e., turtle-doves or young pigeons; however, when of two kinds — e.g., a pair of turtle-doves and a pair of young pigeons. The kohen offered them as obligatory sets, i.e., one above and one below, but did not know which kind he offered first, then — she must bring two — i.e., a turtle-dove and a young pigeon. The pair offered first always counts as her obligatory offering, the other her freewill offering. Accordingly only one of her freewill offering birds became invalid (see above). Now, as it is unknown which kind was offered first, we also do not know whether the turtle-dove or the young pigeon became invalid. And since, as taught earlier (see above 2:5), “Turtle-doves may not be offered with young pigeons nor young pigeons with turtle-doves,” such a doubt now requires her to bring a turtle-dove and a young pigeon as burnt-offerings.

פרשה נדרה If she specified her vow — e.g., she said “I commit myself to bring a pair of turtle-doves if I give birth to a male child,” or “I commit myself to bring a pair of young pigeons if I give birth to a male child,” and forgot which kind she stipulated. If after giving birth she brought two pairs of the same kind and the kohen offered two pigeons above and two below, she must bring another three birds — as burnt-offerings; a bird of the kind she brought to replace the one invalidated (see above) and two of the other kind, which may be the kind she originally vowed to bring. When of one kind — e.g., she brought two pairs of turtle-doves; the pair offered first is her valid obligatory offering, the second pair counts for her vow; even if she vowed to bring turtle-doves, the bird offered below is invalid, and another must be brought to fulfill her vow. However, since she might have vowed to bring a pair of young pigeons, she must now bring another pair of pigeons. This is meant by “she must bring another three pigeons” (see above).

משני מינין When of two kinds — e.g., she brought a pair of turtle-doves and a pair of young pigeons and the kohen offered one below and one above from each pair, and we do not know which pair first and which last, she brings four — birds as burnt-offerings, i.e., a pair of turtle-doves and a pair of young pigeons, as the identity of the second bird offered below and hence invalid is unknown. Moreover, perhaps she vowed a set of turtle-doves but the kohen offered the set of young pigeons last; consequently, she must bring a set of turtle-doves and a young pigeon; or perhaps she vowed to bring a set of young pigeons but the kohen offered the turtle-doves last and thus she must bring a set of young pigeons and a turtle-dove. Therefore, she must bring two sets of bird-offerings, a set of turtle-doves and a set of young pigeons.

קבעה נדרה If she designated her vow — she said, “in addition to my obligatory bird-offering, I commit myself to bring another set” which she specified as turtle-doves or young pigeons, but cannot remember her decision. Hence she must bring three sets of bird offerings; one of any kind for her obligatory offering; a pair of turtle-doves, which she may have vowed; and a pair of pigeons, which she may have vowed; the kohen must offer one bird from her obligatory offering above and one below, all others being offered above as burnt-offerings. Thus, she fulfills her vow with two of the burnt-offerings, the others being freewill offerings. But if she brought but two sets, e.g., four turtle-doves, and of each offering the kohen offered one bird above and one bird below,

צריכה להביא she must bring another five birds — for the second bird offered below is invalid (see above); Now, as she vowed to add another set to her obligatory offering, i.e., a total of three burnt-offerings; even if this involves turtle-doves, only two burnt-offerings were offered, leaving her vow unfulfilled. Therefore she must bring five additional birds for burnt-offerings; two turtle-doves and two pigeons to resolve the doubt about what kind she vowed, and another turtle-dove as her obligatory burnt-offering to fulfill her designated vow requiring her to bring it with her freewill offering. Similarly, had she brought two pairs of young pigeons and the kohen offered one from each pair below and the other above, she must bring two turtle-doves and two pigeons to satisfy her vow and resolve the doubt it entails, and an additional young pigeon for her obligatory burnt-offering to satisfy her designated vow. When is this applicable?

ממין אחד When the birds brought by her are of one kind — see above. However, when the birds are of two different kinds and the kohen offered one bird from each offering above and one below and the identify of the pair offered first is unknown so that she cannot use it for her obligatory offering —

תביא שש she must bring six — birds as burnt-offerings. Two turtle-doves and two young pigeons to resolve the doubt about the kind vowed, and another turtle-dove and young pigeon to resolve the doubt about her obligatory burnt-offering brought with the freewill offering resulting from her designated vow. Since the kind — turtle-doves or young pigeons — offered first is not known, neither is the kind. offered as the sin-offering; and as the obligatory burnt-offering brought with her freewill offering must be of the same kind as the sin-offering, she must bring a turtle-dove and a young pigeon for her obligatory burnt-offering.

נתנתם לכהן If she gave them — i.e., her sets of birds — to the kohen and it is not known what she gave — i.e., whether two sets of turtle-doves, two sets of young pigeons, or a set of turtle-doves and a set of young pigeons; this refers to when her vow was specified and the kind specified was forgotten (see above); and the kohen offered them — i.e., the sets — and the manner in which they were offered is not known, i.e., whether all above, all below, half the number above and half below —

צריכה להביא she must bring another four birds — i.e., two turtle-doves and tow young pigeons for her vow — she may have vowed one kind and brought another, and two — i.e., a turtle-dove and young pigeon — for her obligation — i.e., her obligatory burnt-offering. Both birds of the first set may have been offered below and were of the same kind; and since the obligatory burnt-offering must be of the same kind as the sin-offering whose kind is not known, the doubt requires her to bring a turtle-dove and young pigeon for her obligatory burnt-offering, and one sin-offering — of any kind as both birds of the first set may have been offered above invalidating her sin-offering. We need not ensure that her sin-offering be of the same kind as her original obligatory burnt-offering for as she must now bring two obligatory burnt-offerings owing to the doubt about its kind she will pair the sin-offering with the corresponding kind brought as a burnt-offering.

בן עזאי אומר Ben Azzai says, Two sin-offerings — i.e., a turtle-dove and a young pigeon, in accordance with his view (see above 2:5) that the first is the model. Now all the birds brought first may have been offered above satisfying her obligation to bring a burnt-offering; but as her sin-offering must be of the same kind as her burnt-offering whose kind is not known, she must bring two sin-offerings — one of each kind. Thus Rashi on our mishnah (see Zev. 67b; 68a). However, Rambam’s view shared by Bartenura, differs entirely. Accordingly, one who vows to offer a set of birds may bring a set composed of two kinds. What was taught: “turtle-doves may not be offered with young pigeons nor young pigeons with turtle-doves,” applies only to obligatory bird-offerings. Further, in his view, the set of birds offered first need not necessarily be the obligatory offering as Rashi explains, but may be the freewill offering if so desired. Accordingly: “When of two kinds — she must bring two”: — if she brought two sets of birds of differing kinds and the kohen offered one set below and one above then she must bring another two birds. The set offered above, whether turtle-doves or young pigeons, is her freewill offering; of the set offered below the sin-offering is valid and the burnt-offering invalid. As the kind performed below is unknown and the obligatory burnt-offering must be of the same kind as the sin-offering, she must bring a turtle-dove and a pigeon to complete her obligatory offering. “If she specified her vow” — i.e., at the time of purchase she said, “these for my freewill offering and those for my obligatory offering,” and when given to the kohen they were mixed up with two pigeons being offered below and two above. Now, since the freewill offering may have been offered below — and is thus invalid, and the obligatory offering above — invalidating the sin-offering, “she must bring another three birds.” — When? If of one kind; however, if she brought two kinds, e.g., two turtle-doves for her obligatory offering and two young pigeons for her freewill offering, and in error the kohen offered one set above and one set below, it being unknown which above and which below, whether the turtle-doves of her obligatory offering were offered above, invalidating the sin-offering, or the young pigeons of her freewill below, invalidating both, she must now bring a turtle-dove for a sin-offering and two young pigeons for burnt-offerings; however, the young pigeons may have been offered above as prescribed, and the turtle-doves below invalidating her burnt-offering, and she must bring a turtle-dove for a burnt-offering; thus she has to bring four birds: two turtle-doves for a sin-offering and a burnt-offering and two young pigeons as burnt-offerings. “If she designated her vow,” i.e., when vowing, she designated the kind of her freewill offering, forgot her designation and brought two sets of young pigeons. If at the time of purchase she specified: these are for my freewill offering, and unaware of this, the kohen offered two pigeons above and two below thereby causing four uncertainties in the matter: a) both of the obligatory offerings may have been offered above — thus invalidating the sin-offering, and both of the freewill offerings below — so that both burnt-offerings are invalid; b) both of the freewill offerings may have been offered above as prescribed and both of the obligatory offerings below, thus invalidating the burnt-offering; c) one pigeon of each set may have been offered above and one below thus invalidating the burnt-offering of her freewill offering; d) she may have vowed turtle-doves in which case young pigeons do not satisfy her freewill offering. Hence, she must bring another five birds: two turtle-doves as burnt-offerings, as she may have vowed that kind (uncertainty d); two young pigeons as burnt-offerings because of uncertainties a,b, and c; a turtle-dove as a sin-offering, which may have been invalidated (uncertainty a). When does the above apply? If of one kind. However, if she brought two kinds, specified one set as her freewill offering, forgot which set was specified, and the kohen offered one set above and one set below, it being unknown which above and which below, she must bring six birds: two turtle-doves as burnt-offerings, since she may have vowed and specified that kind, which is invalid when offered below; two young pigeons as burnt-offerings since she may have vowed and specified that kind, which is invalid when offered below; a turtle-dove as a sin-offering, since the kohen may have offered both turtle-doves of her obligatory offering above so that her sin-offering is invalid, and her burnt-offering valid, and she must bring another sin-offering of the same kind; a young pigeon as a sin-offering, since her obligatory offering may have been young pigeons, a sin-offering being invalid when offered above. Hence, she must bring another sin-offering of the same kind as the obligatory burnt-offering. “If she gave them to the kohen and it is not known what she gave and the kohen offered them and it is not known what he did,” i.e., in her vow the woman designated the kind she would bring and specified at the time of purchase which set of birds was her freewill offering, but forgot the designation and specification; she also specified the kind of her obligatory offering, but forgot whether a sheep and a pigeon — a wealthy woman’s offering, or a set of birds; nor does she know what she gave to the kohen, whether two sets of turtle-doves, two sets of young pigeons, or each set of a different kind; nor does the kohen remember how he offered them, whether all above, all below or half above and half below, “she must bring another four birds for her vow,” i.e., two turtle-doves and two young pigeons; since she may have designated turtle-doves but brought young pigeons now, even if turtle-doves were brought they may have been offered below and are invalid; or she may have designated young pigeons but brought turtle-doves, and even if young pigeons were brought they may have been offered below and are invalid, “and two for her obligation,” i.e., one bird for a sin-offering and one for a burnt-offering, both of the same kind, whichever she wishes, since she may have designated that kind but failed to bring it in the first place. “And one sin-offering,” of another kind, i.e., if she brought a set of turtle-doves, and she now must bring a young pigeon as an additional sin-offering or vice-versa, since she may have brought what she designated for her obligation, and both birds were offered above invalidating the sin-offering, which requires her to bring another one to complete the set. Now, even if all burnt-offerings became invalid the above may be paired with one of the burnt-offerings brought because of the uncertainties concerning her vow. Similarly, if she undertook to bring the offering of a wealthy woman and designated a turtle-dove or young pigeon as her sin-offering, she may satisfy that obligation with one of those now brought (see Tiferet Yisrael who questions Rambam’s interpretation; he first presents Rashi’s view, then that of Rambam, Rivah and others).

אמר רבי יהושע Said Rabbi Yehoshua, This is what they have said: while it — the sheep — lives it has one voice — but — when it dies, seven voices; which it is possible to produce as the mishnah explains; this illustrates a woman who gives birth, who when wealthy must bring a sheep as a burnt-offering and a pigeon as a sin-offering or if needy, a set of birds. Although she offered her sacrifice, her vow of an additional set of birds caused a number of uncertainties as to what was specified, what was brought, how the kohen offered them, and whereupon she is now obligated to bring seven birds (in Ben Azzai’s opinion, eight.)

כיצד קולו How are there seven voices? — i.e., how can one produce these from a dead sheep? Its two horns, two trumpets — i.e., the trumpets are made from its horns. Some define the two trumpets as two שופרות. (They would call shofarot trumpets [see Shab. 36a]; however, the actual trumpets were made of silver as explained at the end of Tractate Tamid; according to others, only the trumpets of the kohanim were made of silver, whereas the Levites used horns [Tosafot Zev. 68a]). its two leg-bones, two flutes — i.e., which were made from the leg-bone, its skin for a drum; its large intestines for lyres; its small intestines for harps — i.e., harps were made from its small intestines, And some say, Also its wool for tekhelet — used for the High Priest’s coat which had bells of gold and pomegranates of tekhelet on its hem, and sounds emanated when the pomegranates came in contact with the bells; according to others the bells were located within the pomegranates (Ramban). Since thus the sheep produces eight sounds, Ben Azzai requires the woman to bring eight birds. However, the First Tanna does not include the wool for tekhelet as it is the bell’s clapper that produces the sounds and not the woolen pomegranates.

רבי שמעון בן עקשיה אומר Rabbi Shimon ben Akashia says, Aging ignoramuses, the older they become, the more their minds agitate them — i.e., their thoughts become confused as it is said: (Job 12:20) “He removes the speech of men of trust and takes away the sense of the elders.” God takes away their power of speech and intelligence; the verse deals with the am ha’aretz (i.e., ignorant) (see v. 24) “He takes away the mind from the heads of the am ha’aetz — the people of the land,”

But not so with the Torah elders, who the older they become, the more their minds become settled, as it is said: (ibid. 12) “With aged men — i.e., scholars — there is wisdom — which ignoramuses to not possess and understanding in the length of days” — their perceptions sharpen as time goes by. This statement is appropriate to the conclusion of Seder Kodashim which is also entitled “Wisdom.” It also fits into Rabbi Yehoshua’s statement. Thus, as the sheep though dead produces seven voices, so the elderly scholars, though frail and weak in body, nevertheless grow in wisdom and enhance their cognitive powers thereby perfecting their spiritual attainments (Rambam, Bartenura; see Tiferet Yisrael).

ו. הָאִשָּׁה שֶׁאָמְרָה:

"הֲרֵי עָלַי קֵן כְּשֶׁאֵלֵד זָכָר",

יָלְדָה זָכָר —

מְבִיאָה שְׁתֵּי קִנִּים,

אַחַת לְנִדְרָהּ וְאַחַת לְחוֹבָתָהּ.

נְתָנָתַם לַכֹּהֵן,

וְהַכֹּהֵן צָרִיךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת

שָׁלֹשׁ פְּרִידוֹת מִלְמַעְלָן וְאַחַת מִלְּמַטָּן;

לֹא עָשָׂה כֵּן, אֶלָּא עָשָׂה שְׁתַּיִם לְמַעְלָן וּשְׁתַּיִם לְמַטָּן,

וְלֹא נִמְלַךְ —

צְרִיכָה לְהָבִיא עוֹד פְּרִידָה אַחַת,

וְיַקְרִיבֶנָּה לְמַעְלָן;

מִמִּין אֶחָד.

מִשְּׁנֵי מִינִין —

תָּבִיא שְׁתַּיִם.

פֵּרְשָׁה נִדְרָהּ —

צְרִיכָה לְהָבִיא עוֹד שָׁלֹשׁ פְּרִידוֹת;

מִמִּין אֶחָד.

מִשְּׁנֵי מִינִין —

תָּבִיא אַרְבַּע.

קָבְעָה נִדְרָהּ —

צְרִיכָה לְהָבִיא עוֹד חָמֵשׁ פְּרִידוֹת;

מִמִּין אֶחָד.

מִשְּׁנֵי מִינִין —

תָּבִיא שֵׁשׁ.

נְתָנָתַם לַכֹּהֵן, וְאֵין יָדוּעַ מַה נָּתְנָה,

הָלַךְ הַכֹּהֵן וְעָשָׂה, וְאֵין יָדוּעַ מֶה עָשָׂה —

צְרִיכָה לְהָבִיא עוֹד אַרְבַּע פְּרִידוֹת לְנִדְרָהּ,

וּשְׁתַּיִם לְחוֹבָתָהּ,

וְחַטָּאת אַחַת.

בֶּן עַזַּאי אוֹמֵר: שְׁתֵּי חַטָּאוֹת.

אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ:

זֶה הוּא שֶׁאָמְרוּ:

כְּשֶׁהוּא חַי קוֹלוֹ אֶחָד, וּכְשֶׁהוּא מֵת קוֹלוֹ שִׁבְעָה.

כֵּיצַד קוֹלוֹ שִׁבְעָה?

שְׁתֵּי קַרְנָיו — שְׁתֵּי חֲצוֹצְרוֹת;

שְׁתֵּי שׁוֹקָיו — שְׁנֵי חֲלִילִין;

עוֹרוֹ לְתוֹף;

מֵעָיו לִנְבָלִים;

בְּנֵי מֵעָיו לְכִנּוֹרוֹת.

וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים:

אַף צַמְרוֹ לִתְכֵלֶת.

רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן עֲקַשְׁיָא אוֹמֵר:

זִקְנֵי עַם הָאָרֶץ,

כָּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּזְקִינִין —

דַּעְתָּן מִטָּרֶפֶת עֲלֵיהֶן,

שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (איוב יב, כ):

"מֵסִיר שָׂפָה לְנֶאֱמָנִים,

וְטַעַם זְקֵנִים יִקָּח".

אֲבָל זִקְנֵי תוֹרָה אֵינָן כֵּן,

אֶלָּא כָּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּזְקִינִין —

דַּעְתָּן מִתְיַשֶּׁבֶת עֲלֵיהֶן,

שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שם שם, יב):

"בִּישִׁישִׁים חָכְמָה,

וְאֹרֶךְ יָמִים תְּבוּנָה".
